The article traces the timeline of the takeover bid, which began in November 2022 when the Glazer family, who had controlled the club since 2005, announced they were open to selling shares. The bidding process was initially expected to conclude before the summer transfer window, but it dragged on, prompting fan protests and revealing the Glazers’ reluctance to sell.

Ratcliffe, who has previously attempted to buy Chelsea, emerged as the main rival to Qatari Sheikh Jassim bin Al Thani, who withdrew from the bidding process, clearing the way for Ratcliffe to move forward. He has now agreed in principle to purchase a 25% stake in Manchester United for £1.3 billion, though the exact terms and timing remain uncertain. The board meeting scheduled for Thursday is expected to discuss the proposal, though it is not guaranteed to be put to a vote, as several key details are still being negotiated.

Ratcliffe seeks not only a financial stake but also executive control and the appointment of his own sporting director, with Paul Mitchell being a leading candidate. He also plans to appoint Dave Brailsford, a renowned sports director, to oversee the club’s sporting strategy. Additionally, Ratcliffe aims to upgrade Old Trafford to a 90,000-seat stadium and is seeking to ratify the deal in time for the January transfer window, though financial constraints due to FFP regulations may limit spending.

Despite his age (71), Ratcliffe’s vision is centered on long-term stability and success for the club, rather than a short-term turnaround. The article also notes that the Glazers will remain in place, which has been met with fan discontent, but Ratcliffe’s ultimate goal is to eventually remove them and take full control of the club.

In summary, the article outlines the complex, high-stakes, and emotionally charged process of Manchester United’s potential transition from Glazer ownership to Ratcliffe’s INEOS Group, highlighting the political, financial, and sporting implications of this pivotal moment in the club’s history.
